questions.text: The diagram says each forward move is 'person approves'. Who is that person, where do they approve (what tool or screen), and what exactly happens when they do? Does something change billing_mode?
questions.about: Forward moves are one step at a time, each made by a person

questions.text: What is the 'rollout controller'? What does it do each day or event, and who writes the billing_mode flag: the controller or the approver?
questions.about: Where the rollout state lives: rollout record written only by the rollout controller

questions.text: In shadow, what does the nightly job compare per customer, and where do the mismatch counts and the 7-day streak get recorded? Who counts the 5000 invoices?
questions.about: shadow: nightly job compares the two engines per customer

questions.text: In both, how is it decided which engine charges a given customer's period, and how does the idempotency key stop the old engine from charging a period the new engine already charged?
questions.about: both: the new engine charges and writes the ledger; double-charge guard

questions.text: In the automatic trigger, what counts as a 'charge failure' (declined card, provider error, timeout)? What does the controller do the moment the threshold is crossed, and what stops charges immediately?
questions.about: rb_freeze: freeze new engine and stop new charges and ledger writes

questions.text: In rb_reconcile, how is the 'due-but-uncharged list' built, and where is it stored? What is the old engine's 'queue' that it is handed to?
questions.about: Step 3 mark charged periods and build due-but-uncharged list

questions.text: In rb_handover, what are 'gates reset' and when is billing_mode finally set to old_only? Is the flag unchanged during steps 1-4, and what do the engines do meanwhile?
questions.about: Step 5 old engine charges due-but-uncharged periods and gates reset

questions.text: In new_only, what is the '35-day log' of usage events, who keeps it, and why does the old engine need those events to catch up?
questions.about: new_only: rollback window is open until day 35

answers.text: The approver is a person recorded in the rollout record. The brief names no person or tool, so the tool or screen is open question 7. The approval and its reference are recorded, and then the controller writes billing_mode to the next mode. So yes, the approval changes billing_mode, through the controller.

The rollout controller is the program that owns the rollout record and the flag. Each night it runs the comparison and updates the streaks. Continuously it watches charge failures per 10-minute window. When a person approves a move, it applies the next mode. During a rollback it runs the steps. The controller is the only writer of billing_mode. The approver never writes the flag directly. The brief says only a person makes forward moves, and one writer keeps the audit log complete.

Per customer, the nightly job compares the old engine's invoice total with the new engine's shadow invoice total for the same period. A mismatch is a difference of more than one cent. The job writes per-day counts of invoices compared and mismatched. The controller copies those into the rollout record and updates the streak. The job does the counting of the 5,000 invoices. Whether that 5,000 is cumulative or per day is open question 9.

Only one engine charges at a time, and billing_mode decides which. Engines read it before each charge. In both, the old engine does not charge, so it cannot charge a period the new engine charged. The idempotency key covers an overlap, such as a retry or a flip. Both engines use the same key per customer, period and invoice version, and the provider and the ledger refuse a second charge or record with that key.

A charge failure is any charge attempt not confirmed as successful: a decline, a provider error or a timeout. A timeout counts until its outcome is resolved, because it may still have charged. When the rate crosses 2%, the controller sets the rollback to step 1 and writes the freeze marker. The new engine checks the marker before every charge, as it does the flag, so it stops at its next check. Attempts in flight are resolved in step 2. The denominator and minimum count are open question 4.

The list is built in step 5, from ledger invoices with no successful charge record. It is built after catch-up so that invoices for skipped events are included. Building it in step 3 would miss those. The list is held in the rollback step data in the rollout record. The old engine's queue is the list of periods it charges first, before its normal run, with the same keys. Where the queue is stored is open question 10.

billing_mode is not changed during steps 1 to 4. The freeze marker stops the new engine. In both, the old engine keeps computing into the shadow store without charging. In new_only, the old engine runs catch-up without charging. Nothing charges during steps 1 to 4. billing_mode is set to old_only at the start of step 5, before the old engine charges, because the old engine does not charge in both or new_only. The gates reset when the rollback finishes.

The brief says the usage event log is kept for 35 days, but it does not name who keeps the log. That is open question 8. The old engine needs the skipped events because it computes invoices from usage events. In new_only it stopped, so it has no invoices for events since entry. Without reprocessing, the old engine cannot bill those periods, and after day 35 the events are gone.

questions.text: What does it mean for a mismatch to be resolved, and who resolves it and records that?
questions.about: both: gate to new_only needs no unresolved mismatches

questions.text: In a rollback from both, the ledger invoices were written by the new engine. When the old engine charges them, how does it get the same invoice version in the key, so the provider and ledger treat it as the same charge?
questions.about: Step 5 Hand over: old engine charges the queued periods with the same idempotency keys

questions.text: When is the freeze marker cleared, and what does the new engine do if it reads the marker mid-charge, after sending a request to the provider but before getting a result?
questions.about: Step 1 Stop the new engine: freeze marker

questions.text: Where is the mark on a charged period stored, and how does the old engine read it to skip those periods?
questions.about: Step 3 Mark charged periods

questions.text: At the start of step 5, billing_mode flips to old_only. How does the system ensure the new engine, which is already frozen, cannot charge during the flip, and what if the old engine's queued charges start before the flip is visible to all workers?
questions.about: Rules for all modes: engines read billing_mode before each charge

questions.text: Who or what runs the nightly comparison job, and who notices when it did not run?
questions.about: Nightly comparison fails or does not run

answers.text: A mismatch is resolved when its cause is written to the audit log and the next nightly comparison shows that customer's totals agree within one cent. The controller records the resolution. The gate needs a state the controller can check, and a fix without a re-comparison would not show that the fix works. Who investigates is open question 11, because the brief does not say.

It does not need a different version. Step 5 charges the ledger invoice that already exists, with the version and key it was written under. The old engine does not recompute it. The ledger is the system of record, and a recomputed invoice could carry a different version and so a second charge, which the brief rules out.

The freeze marker is cleared in step 5, after every worker reads old_only, and only when the rollback finishes. The new engine checks the marker before it sends each request. If it has already sent a request, it does not cancel it, because cancelling could leave an unknown outcome. The outcome goes to step 2, which looks it up by idempotency key and never retries under a new key.

The mark is the success written to the ledger's charge record under the period's idempotency key. The ledger is the system of record and already holds the key. The old engine reads that record before each charge and skips a period that has one.

No charge can happen during the flip. In both, the old engine does not charge, and the freeze marker stops the new engine. The old queue starts only after every worker reads old_only, so a worker still on both cannot cause a charge. This is the reason for the wait in step 5.

The brief does not say who schedules the nightly job or who is notified when it does not run. The file records the missed day, which resets the streak. Who runs the job and who is alerted is open question 12.

questions.text: In shadow, rollback step 1 sets billing_mode to old_only and stops shadow writes, then goes straight to old_only. Is the flag flip there also confirmed by all workers, or is it immediate?
questions.about: rb_shadow: Step 1 set billing_mode old_only and stop shadow writes

questions.text: In both, the new engine charges. After the freeze marker is set and before step 5, who charges customers whose periods come due? Do those customers just wait until handover?
questions.about: Step 1 Stop the new engine: Failed charges stay queued as due

questions.text: The rollback path says it 'does not move forward' and always ends in old_only. After step 5, what is the exact next action? Does the rollout record go back to old_only with a person approving old_only to shadow again?
questions.about: Rules for all modes: After any rollback, the gates reset

questions.text: Step 5 says the old engine charges due periods from the ledger invoice as written. In a rollback from both, the shadow store holds the old engine's own invoices. Which invoice wins when the shadow and ledger invoices differ, and who decides?
questions.about: Step 5 Hand over / Shadow invoices are never charged

questions.text: What does a person see or do when a manual rollback is started? Who may start it, and how is it recorded?
questions.about: Rollback steps: A person can start it by hand at any time

questions.text: In step 2, what happens if the provider says it has no record of a charge with that key (not charged), or does not answer? Is the period treated as due and left in the queue?
questions.about: Step 2 Resolve in-flight charges

answers.text: The flag flip is not waited on for a rollback from shadow. In shadow the old engine already charges and writes the ledger, and it charges the same way in old_only, so no charge depends on which value a worker reads. The new engine is not charging in shadow, so it has nothing to freeze and stopping shadow writes is enough. Step 1 now says this. The rules line that said the old engine charges only in old_only conflicted with the brief (the old engine charges in shadow too), so I corrected it.

Nobody charges during steps 1 to 4. Customers whose periods come due in that window wait until step 5, when the old engine charges the due list. The reason is that the brief forbids a double charge, and an in-flight charge with an unknown outcome could still have succeeded, so charging early is not safe. The brief sets no limit on how long that wait can be; this is a hole for the report, not something I can decide from the brief.

After step 5 the rollout is at old_only, its start state, and the freeze marker is cleared. Nothing moves forward until a person approves old_only to shadow, as for any forward move. The 7-day count starts when shadow is entered. The brief states the gates reset and that a person always makes forward moves. No separate approval of old_only is needed beyond that.

The ledger invoice wins. The brief says shadow invoices are never charged, and the ledger is the system of record, so nobody decides case by case. In a rollback from both, the new engine wrote the ledger invoices and the old engine's shadow invoices never override them. A disagreement between the two engines is what the nightly comparison reports; how it is investigated is not in the brief and is an open question. Checking this also showed that catch-up in new_only may write ledger invoices for periods the new engine already invoiced, which the brief does not cover. I added that as an open question.

The brief says on-call can start a rollback by hand at any time within the 35-day limit, so on-call is who may start it. The start is recorded in the rollout record and the audit log, since every controller change is. What on-call sees on screen is not in the brief; it belongs with the approver tool question, which is open.

If the provider has no record under that key, the charge is recorded as not charged. The period stays due and step 5 charges it under the same key, which is safe only if the provider would hold a record of a successful charge under that key. If the provider does not answer, the outcome is unknown, so the period is neither charged nor queued, the lookup is retried, and step 2 does not finish until every lookup is answered. Hole: a request sent before the freeze could still arrive after a not-found answer, and the same key stops a second charge only if the provider keeps keys long enough. This depends on the provider-lookup open question.

questions.text: In step 5, how does the controller know that every worker reads old_only? Do workers report back, or does the controller poll something?
questions.about: Step 5 Hand over: Wait until every worker reads old_only

questions.text: What happens if one worker never confirms old_only (crashed or stuck)? Does the wait go on forever, and who is alerted?
questions.about: Step 5 Hand over: wait for all workers

questions.text: What is a worker here, and what does it do? Is it the same thing as an engine, or does each engine run several workers that each charge customers?
questions.about: Rules for all modes: Engines read billing_mode before each charge

questions.text: When the old engine charges the due list in step 5, what happens if a charge fails or times out? Does it count as a charge failure, and can it start another rollback?
questions.about: Step 5 Hand over: old engine charges each due-list period

questions.text: In both, the old engine writes invoices to the shadow store. What does 'no unresolved mismatches for 14 days' mean if a new mismatch appears on day 10? Does the 14-day count restart?
questions.about: both: gate to new_only is 14 days with no unresolved mismatches

questions.text: Is a rollback already in progress affected if the failure rate crosses 2% again, or if on-call starts a second manual rollback? Which one runs?
questions.about: Rollback steps: Each step is idempotent and resumable

answers.text: The brief does not say how the controller learns that every worker reads old_only. Workers reporting their mode is one possible way, but that is a mechanism the brief does not state. I did not invent one. The file now says the wait has no timeout. The reporting method is added as open question 14.

The wait does not time out. A timeout would let the old engine charge while a worker may still read both, which is the double-charge risk the brief forbids. The rollout stays on the rollback path until the wait ends. Who is alerted is not in the brief, so it is part of open question 14.

The brief says 'Billing workers run the old engine', so a worker is a billing process that runs an engine and reads billing_mode before each charge. I defined it in Terms. The brief does not say how many workers each engine runs, so I did not state a number.

A failed or timed-out due-list charge stays due. A timeout is first resolved by the step 2 lookup, and the retry uses the same idempotency key, never a new one. It does not start another rollback. The automatic trigger watches only new-engine charges in both or new_only, and by step 5 the rollout is no longer in those modes. A manual rollback can start only from shadow, both or new_only, so not from old_only. Reason: the brief allows a rollback only from those modes, and a due charge must not be dropped.

The 14-day count does not restart on a mismatch. The brief asks for 14 days in both with no unresolved mismatches. I read the mismatch part as a check on the day of approval. A day-10 mismatch that is resolved by then (cause logged and the next comparison agrees) does not block the gate. Reason: a resolved mismatch is closed, and restarting the count would hold the gate for a problem already fixed. A mismatch still unresolved on approval day means the gate is not met. The file now says this.

Only one rollback runs at a time. The rollout stays on the rollback path until step 5, so a second failure-rate trigger or a second manual start is logged and ignored. The running rollback continues and ends in old_only. Reason: two rollbacks running steps at once could both charge the due list, which the brief rules out. The brief is silent on this, so this is my decision.

teachbacks.text:
1. Starting state. The rollout begins in `old_only`. The old engine reads usage events, computes invoices, writes them to the billing ledger and charges customers through the payment provider. The new engine is off. `billing_mode` is the one global flag in the config service. The rollout record sits beside it and holds the mode, the day-35 clock, the streak, the approval references and the rollback state. Only the rollout controller writes either of them, and every change goes to the audit log.

2. Move to shadow. A person approves the move and the approval is recorded. Then the controller writes `billing_mode = shadow`. The approver never writes the flag. Forward moves go one step at a time with no skips, and no forward move is automatic. The 7-day count starts when `shadow` is entered.

3. A normal run in shadow. Usage events come from the usage event log. The old engine computes invoices, writes them to the ledger and charges through the provider, as before. The new engine reads the same events and writes its invoices only to the shadow store. It never charges and never writes the ledger. Engines read `billing_mode` before each charge and never cache it, because a stale read during a flip is the main double-charge risk. Both engines send the same idempotency key (customer, billing period, invoice version) to the provider. The provider and the ledger refuse a second charge or record with the same key.

4. Nightly comparison. A nightly job compares the two engines' invoices per customer. A mismatch is a total that differs by more than one cent. The controller reads the results and updates the streak, the invoice count and the mismatch counts in the rollout record. If the job fails or does not run, that day does not count and the streak resets. This is a proposal, and the controller records the missed run. New-engine errors in shadow are recorded and never trigger a rollback.

5. Gate to both. The gate is 7 consecutive days with a mismatch rate under 0.1% and at least 5,000 invoices compared. When it is met, a person approves and the controller writes `both`.

6. A normal run in both. The new engine now charges and writes the ledger. The old engine keeps computing every invoice into the shadow store and does not charge. The comparison continues. The automatic rollback trigger is armed. It fires when new-engine charge failures exceed 2% in any 10-minute window.

7. Gate to new_only. The gate is 14 days in `both` with no unresolved mismatches, plus Finance sign-off. Unresolved mismatches are checked on the day the person approves. A mismatch resolved before then does not block the gate, and the 14-day count does not restart. After approval, the controller writes `new_only` and starts the day-35 clock.

8. new_only and retired. In `new_only` the new engine does everything. The old engine stops computing, so it skips every usage event from entry on. The rollback window stays open until day 35. On or after day 35, with no rollback started, a person decommissions the old engine. The state is then `retired`, which is terminal.

9. Rollback start. A rollback can start only from `shadow`, `both` or `new_only`. On-call can start it by hand. It also starts automatically in `both` or `new_only` when charge failures exceed 2% over 10 minutes. The start goes into the rollout record and the audit log. Only one rollback runs at a time, and a second start or trigger is logged and ignored. Each step is idempotent and resumable. The rollout stays on the rollback path until step 5 finishes.

10. Rollback from shadow. This runs step 1 only. The controller sets `billing_mode` to `old_only` and stops shadow writes. No wait is needed, because the old engine charges the same way in both modes and the new engine was not charging.

11. Rollback from both or new_only, step 1 (freeze). The controller sets the freeze marker in the rollout record. The new engine checks the marker before sending each charge request. When it is set, the new engine stops new charges and ledger writes. A request already sent is not cancelled, and its outcome goes to step 2. `billing_mode` does not change during steps 1 to 4. Nothing charges during this window. Failed charges stay queued as due, and any period that comes due waits for step 5.

12. Step 2 (resolve unknown charges). For each charge with an unknown outcome, including a timeout, the controller asks the payment provider about the idempotency key and records the answer. It never retries under a new key. If the provider has no record of the key, the charge is recorded as not charged. The period stays due and step 5 charges it under the same key. If the provider does not answer, the outcome stays unknown, the lookup is retried on the next run, and the period is not queued. Step 2 does not finish until every lookup is answered.

13. Step 3 (mark charged periods). For each successfully charged period, the success is written to the ledger's charge record under the period's idempotency key. The old engine checks this record before every charge and skips any period that has one.

14. Step 4 (catch-up, from new_only only). The old engine reprocesses the usage events it skipped, inside the 35-day log. It writes the resulting invoices to the ledger and charges nothing. This must finish before the oldest skipped event expires. If it does not, the rollback cannot be completed from events.

15. Step 5 (hand over).
 - The controller builds the due list: the ledger invoices that have no charge record. It holds the list in the rollout record's rollback data. Shadow invoices are never charged, and the ledger invoice wins if the two differ.
 - The controller sets `billing_mode` to `old_only`, then waits with no timeout until every worker reads `old_only`.
 - It clears the freeze marker.
 - The old engine charges each due-list period from its ledger invoice as written, with that invoice's version and key. It does not recompute. This queue runs before the old engine's normal run.
 - A charge that fails or times out stays due. A timeout is first resolved by the step 2 lookup, and any retry uses the same key. These charges do not count toward the automatic trigger and do not start a rollback.

16. After the rollback. The system is in `old_only` with the gates reset. Nothing moves forward until a person approves the move to `shadow`, and the 7-day count restarts from there.

17. Other failures. If the config service is unreachable, workers keep their last-read mode, raise an alert, and the rollout does not advance. If a rollback or trigger happens after day 35 in `new_only`, the controller pages on-call and waits for a person's decision. A manual start in `old_only` is not allowed. A mismatch blocks the next gate but does not trigger a rollback by itself. If a rollback step fails midway, it resumes on retry and the due charges stay queued.
gaps: Where the rollout record lives and who owns it (open question 1). I can't say what the controller reads and writes at each step.

How many billing workers each engine runs, and how a worker is scheduled or triggered. I can't say what starts a run, how a run turns into a charge request, or how a failed charge gets back in the queue.

The mechanism that detects an unknown or timed-out charge, and who or what flags it for step 2. It is also unclear how the controller measures the 2% charge-failure rate: denominator, minimum attempt count, and whether a timeout counts as a failure (open question 4).
Whether the payment provider can look up a charge by idempotency key, and how long it keeps keys (open question 5). Step 2 depends on this.
How the controller learns that every worker reads `old_only`, and who is alerted if a worker never confirms (open question 14).
Where the old engine's queue of due periods is stored, and exactly how the due list is handed to it (open question 10).
Whether catch-up writes a new invoice version for a period the new engine already invoiced in `new_only`, which could make a second chargeable invoice (open question 13).

What happens when a rollback is triggered after day 35 (open question 3). The document only says the controller pages on-call and waits for a person's decision. It does not say what that decision can be.
Whether the 5,000-invoice minimum applies across the 7 days or to each day (open question 9).
Who schedules the nightly comparison, and who is alerted when it fails (open question 12).
Who investigates a mismatch and where the cause is recorded. The audit log is implied but not confirmed (open question 11).
Which tool or screen the approver and on-call use, and what an approval record contains (open question 7).
Who owns and keeps the 35-day usage event log (open question 8).

How a worker or the new engine learns the freeze marker is set, beyond 'checks the marker before sending each charge request'. For example, how the controller moves the rollout from one rollback step to the next and what triggers each step to run.
How shadow-store writes are stopped and how the 'gates reset' is done, beyond the statement that they are reset.
